title: Fisher of Rochester: agrees veniality is of mercy; difference is grace-flight
source_text: XVI. His consentanea docet Joannes Roffensis in Anglia Episcopus, in refutatione assertionis Lutheranae, ad articulum trigesimum secundum. Ubi postquam induxit Lutherum dicentem, veniale peccatum non natura sua, sed Dei misericordia tale esse, subjungit, Quod veniale peccatum solum ex Dei misericordia tale sit, in hoc tecum sentio. Sed quoniam & nos mortale quoque peccatum per Dei misericordiam fieri posse veniale credimus, vellem apertius nobis exponeres quid ipse discriminis arbitreris inter mortale & veniale peccatum statui debere. Illud vero discrimen ipse postea in eo constituit, quod mortale protinus effugit ab animo gratiam, & in odio Dei constituit ipsum peccatorem; at veniale non ita. Et paulo post concedit veniale peccatum esse damnabile; si districte judicetur. Inde vero negat sequi veniale peccatum mortale esse. Nam, inquit, mortale peccatum fugat a nobis gratiam, propter quam & merito damnandum venit, non autem identidem veniale. Quod discrimen abunde satis est, ut veniale dici mortale nequeat.
pass_a_gloss: Things agreeing with these John Fisher, bishop in England, teaches in the refutation of the Lutheran assertion, at article thirty-two. Where after he has introduced Luther saying that venial sin is such not by its nature but by God’s mercy, he subjoins: That venial sin is such only from God’s mercy, in this I agree with you. But since we also believe that even mortal sin can become venial through God’s mercy, I would wish you to set out more openly for us what difference you yourself judge ought to be established between mortal and venial sin. But that difference he himself afterwards establishes in this, that mortal at once drives grace from the mind and sets the sinner himself in the hatred of God; but venial not so. And a little later he grants that venial sin is damnable if it be judged strictly. Yet from that he denies it follows that venial sin is mortal. For, he says, mortal sin drives grace from us, on account of which it also deservedly comes to be damned, but not likewise venial. Which difference is abundantly enough that venial cannot be called mortal.
pass_b_english: Fisher grants Luther that ‘venial’ is of mercy, yet marks the real divide: mortal drives out grace and sets one in God’s hatred; venial does not.
Strictly judged, venial may be damnable—but that does not make it mortal in Fisher’s sense.
